title: Massachusetts Makes It Official: August 15 Is Now India Day in the Commonwealth
excerpt: Governor Maura Healey's proclamation formalises the recognition of Indian Independence Day as a state-level celebration, as New England's diaspora community prepares for 2026 festivities.
body:
• Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey has proclaimed August 15 as "India Day in the Commonwealth," recognising the Indian American community's cultural, economic, and civic contributions to the state.
  • The declaration followed the 4th International India Day Parade at Boston Harbor on August 10, 2025, hosted by the Foundation of Indian Americans – New England (FIA-NE) with representatives from over 20 nations.
  • Bollywood actor-filmmaker Jugal Hansraj served as Grand Marshal, with themed floats honouring George Washington, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's 150th birth anniversary.
  • With India Day 2026 approaching on August 15, the India Association of Greater Boston will host "Colors of India – Stories That Inspire" at NARA Park Amphitheater in Acton, Massachusetts.

Massachusetts has officially enshrined August 15 as "India Day in the Commonwealth," a formal state proclamation that elevates what was once a community celebration into an institutionally recognised moment of cultural pride. As the 2026 date approaches, the declaration stands as one of the most visible acts of civic recognition for Indian Americans in the northeastern United States.

How It Happened

Governor Maura Healey issued the proclamation on August 13, 2025, two days before India's Independence Day. It came on the heels of the 4th International India Day Parade, hosted on August 10 at Boston Harbor by the Foundation of Indian Americans – New England (FIA-NE).

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2084858717670183009

The parade drew representatives from more than 20 nations and featured Bollywood actor and filmmaker Jugal Hansraj as Grand Marshal. Themed floats honoured figures spanning both American and Indian history — George Washington alongside Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose — with a special tribute marking the 150th birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Officials from the Boston Mayor's office and the Indian consulate joined the ribbon-cutting ceremony.

"This proclamation not only signifies India's journey to independence but also showcases the vibrant cultural diversity that enriches Massachusetts."

— FIA New England, in a statement thanking Governor Healey

Why It Matters

The proclamation's significance extends beyond symbolism. It represents a formal acknowledgment by the state government of the Indian American community's growing economic and civic footprint in Massachusetts. The state is home to major concentrations of Indian-origin professionals in healthcare, technology, academia, and entrepreneurship — sectors that drive significant economic activity in the Greater Boston area.

Massachusetts has a history of such proclamations, with former Governor Charlie Baker having recognised India Day in 2022 during the country's 75th independence anniversary celebrations. Healey's declaration makes it a recurring institutional fixture rather than a one-off gesture.

The Indian Consulate in New York formally thanked the governor, describing the proclamation as an affirmation of the community's contributions and a bridge between two democratic traditions.

India Day 2026: What's Planned

With August 15, 2026, approaching, the India Association of Greater Boston (IAGB) has announced its flagship cultural festival, "Colors of India – Stories That Inspire." The event will be held from 2:30 to 7:30 p.m. at NARA Park Amphitheater in Acton, Massachusetts — a new venue chosen for its open-air setting, ample parking, and family-friendly accessibility.

Under the leadership of IAGB President Nilesh Agrawal, the festival will feature classical, folk, Bollywood, and fusion performances, community booths showcasing art and small businesses, authentic Indian cuisine, and family-friendly interactive activities.

A Growing Pattern of Recognition

The Massachusetts proclamation is part of a broader pattern of Indian diaspora communities securing formal civic recognition across the United States. From flag-raising ceremonies at state houses to cultural festivals that draw thousands, Indian Americans are translating demographic and economic influence into institutional visibility.

For the estimated 4.2 million people of Indian descent in the United States — the second-largest immigrant group in the country — moments like India Day provide an anchor for cultural identity and civic belonging, particularly for younger South Asian Americans navigating dual identities in American public life.
